summary: Instrumental playing is secured by flute names and b-marked instruments (PrS 6/18; 57/23; MAC Old lady and a bird/45). Separate moḥe ... bu ṭambər plus zomər supports vocal singing (JTM 5.2/74). Bare wedding coordination with dancing alone does not resolve singing against playing.
Song topic is marked by ʕal (PrS 45/45; 56/16), language by b- or a bare language name, and audience by l- or a suffix. These are ordinary valency variants, not idioms.

Infectum-wa covers habitual past (11/234) and imagined performance with g- plus -wa (MAC Ditin Hazar/30). g- also appears in past or general performance scenes; its spelling alone is not evidence for absolute future time.

Existing Part act. and Infinitiv examples have null sense labels in the parsed entry. Their broad music context must not be silently counted as sense 1. Inherited boxes remain intact, including nominal zamoro under Part act.
No specialized light-verb idiom is established. qayso du zmoro names the story's singing wood compositionally and is documented as an extension, not a new idiom.
Repeated tokens and three compact source-free records retain separate ledger lines; only records supplied with verses are independently checked.

Jan is predominantly recorded interview discourse here, not uniformly learned written syntax. Infectum-wa is habitual or an ability complement; -wa/-wo and plural zəmriwa/zəmriwo vary by speaker. Round 1 already established this box.
bu femo zəmriwo contrasts vocal performance with moḥanwo kamanča/dənnaga/zərnaye (Jan 1.24/1234). Instrument names elsewhere cannot by themselves turn singing into I.2.
Language may be bare or b-marked; song content may be a cognate nominal or a relative head. Incomplete b phrases at Jan 1.38/1659 and 1.59/2941 are preserved without supplying a language.

Jan 2.16 contrasts I zəmarle (unassimilated r) and zumarre with three m-prefixed forms. The provisional II section records repeated morphology; no separate sacred/secular, language or beneficiary sense is supported.
Jan 2.8/2017 and /2019 have identical supplied verses; preserve separate occurrence records without duplicate examples. Part act. zamore is an agent noun under the inherited box label.
All added English is supplied project machine translation. For example hedi at Jan 1.59/2946 and di ʕade at Jan 2.8/1893 are not assigned meanings from that English alone.
Does the existing Infinitiv example zmr.I.t.infinitiv.1 (4/54) belong to sense 2 or a broader music-making category? Its parsed sense is null; no reassignment made.
Does zamoro in 2/105 denote a singer specifically or a musician more broadly? Existing Part act. label and wording are preserved.
Is PrS 1/35 the correct replacement for prs 3/21 on zmr.I.t.preterit.3, or an independently numbered parallel? Edition verification is needed before changing the citation.
Can native speakers resolve vocal singing versus instrumental playing in the unqualified wedding passages and 81/88? No new meaning is inferred from translation alone.

Do mzamri/kəmzamri/mzamarre in Jan 2.16 represent learned II, a written borrowing, or an I variant? The new II section is explicitly provisional; its Preterit is unattested.
Does the second zəmriwo at Jan 3.50/1429 mean vocal singing or instrumental playing? No I.2 example is published from this unresolved token.
At Jan 1.59/2934, is az zamore the singers as subject rather than the songs as object?

Correct imperative las to lass
rationale: The imperative of lassen is lass, not the past-tense form las of lesen. The edition at 11/212 confirms “lass mich mal hören”.

summary: Restore plural musicians with were
rationale: The singular musician conflicts with were. The quoted am=məṭərb and ko-zəmri are plural, and the edition likewise has plural die Zigeuner spielten auf; restore the missing plural s while retaining the editors’ choice musicians.

summary: Magical sticks/trees, personified water and radios act as singers; audible singing remains the meaning, without new numbered senses.
Narrative animals play instruments, with the same b-marked instrumental construction as human players.
Further support for round-1 nonhuman/inanimate singer extension: a gramophone kzəmro and creatures zəmriwo until dawn. No repeated new sense or idiom.
Antiphonal work singing is made explicit by ḥa zumarwo w ḥa madʕarwo; ʕam ḥḏoḏe and the paired practice called čəfta remain compositional, rather than new numbered senses.
